   FACT: THESE DESIGNS, AND LATER ONES ARE REAL                        have the power to "coast" long distances,
                                                                       thus saving on fuel consumption.
                                                                           Direction of the aircraft and its veloc­
                                                                       ity, in turn, evidently are controlled by
                                                                       the angle at which the jet nozzles are
                                                                       tilted, the number operating, the power
                                                                       applied. By choosing which nozzles to
                                                                       turn on or off and the angle of tilt, the
                                                                       pilot could make the saucer rise or de­
                                                                       scend vertically, hover, fly straight ahead.
                                                                       or make sharp turns. A right-angle turn.
                                                                       for example, could be made by turning
                                                                       off the rear jets, turning on the side and
                                                                       fiont nozzles. Great speed can be ob­
                                                                       tained by focusing to the rear all nozzles
                                                                       i11 the after half of the aircraft. With all
                                                                       nozzles pointed downward. the saucer
                                                                       could rise straight off the ground, and,
                                                                       with less power. could descend the same
                                                                       way.
                                                                          That is the explanation, based on ac­
                                                                       cepted principles of aerodynamics, given
                                                                       by an authoritative engineer as the likely
                                                                       answer to how these saucer aircraft oper­
                                                                       ate. As evidence that this explanation is
                                                                       correct, there are these actual cases of
                                                                       publicly observed saucer behavior:
                                                                           Rows of window-like openings around
                                                                       the rims of saucers traveling at more
                                                                       than 500 miles an hour are ,mentioned in
                                                                       several cloc11mcnted reports. In all cases,
                                                                       these "windows" glowed as if they were
                                                                       jet-nozzle openings. The most recent of
         DISK-LIKE NAVY FLOUNDER PROJECT WAS 'DROPPED'                 these reports was made last month by
                                                                       two experienced pilots of the Chicago
                                                                       and Southern Air Lines, who passed
                                                                       within 1.000 feet of a saucer traveling
                                                                       over Arkansas. .<\nother similar report
                                                                       was m,1de bv two Eastern Air Lines
                                                                       pilots who n,11:rowly missed colliding with
                                                                       a saucer in July, 1948, while flying a
                                                                       DC-3 over Georgia.
                                                                           Saucers' abilitv to hover in mid-air,
                                                                       accelerate at t1:emcndous speed, and
                                                                       then rise almost vertically is described in
                                                                       several reports, one documented by Air
                                                                       Force officers at Fort Knox, Ky. That
                                                                       saucer, seen by dozens of officers at the
                                                                       post, was chased by three military pilots
                                                                       flying fast F-51s. The saucer quickly out­
                                                                       maneuvered the µlanes.
                                                                           Speed of one saucer was measured by
                                                                       ground instruments in the White Sands
                                                                       case at well over the speed of sound,
                                                                       indicating the use of a number of jet
                                                                       engines. Cruising speed has been esti­
                                                                       mated in other cases at 200 to 600 miles
                                                                       an hour.
                                                                           What it all adds up to is this: Flying
                                                                       saucers being observed in many parts
                                                                       of the U.S. are not mysterious visitors
                                                                       from Mars. They are actual planes, sound­
                                                                       ly engineered on principles developed by
                                                                       U.S. in wartime. By using this new design,
                                                                       they can do things that no conventional
                                                                       aircraft can be expected to approach.

MAN FROM 'ETHERIA
        Few San Diegans know that a small office on Adams
     Avenue harbors almost as much data on flying discs
     as the Air Forces.
       There, behind a desk piled high with reports, sits a
     weary, heavy-jowled man who has long waged a
     battle with Washington to release "the truth" about
     mysterious sky objects. This week he produced what
     the Air Forces have not yet come up with: photographic
     evidence.
        Released to the general public exclusively in POINT,
     one of the pix would have the Air Forces up in the air
     or down in the mouth: a 27-inch "aluminum" man, pur­
     portedly captured after crashing near Mexico City last
     spring.
       Although not himself the man behind the camera,
     Meade Layne offers the photographs as unchallenge­
     able proof that men of disc-tinction are real.
        Layne is director of the Borderland Sciences Re­
     search Associates, and his office serves as a clearing
     house for disc data.
        According to Layne, the pictures were suppressed in
     this country. Smuggled to Germany, they appeared in
     a Cologne newspaper. An associate in that city dis­
     patched reproductions to Layne.
        Layne's report tells him a disc appeared over Monu­
     ment Valley, Arizona, at 9:45 p.m. last March 21, and
     was photographed by Flak Sgt. D. Ussel, of the 13th
     Airborne Division. Seconds later, flak rockets hit the
     object and it disintegrated in a shower of fireworks.
14
                                  Don't turn the page
                                  without reading the
                                  words below. There's
                                  a shocker waiting for
                                  you ...

"About 20 silvery capsules fell lo the ground," Ussel declared.
   Enter the Aluminum Man.
   He was sealed in one of the silver capsules that fell when
a similar disc cracked up in Mexico, reported Layne's source,
identified as "eye-witness G-Mcm McKenerich, of Phoenix."
   Said McKenerich: "I was astounded by the importance of
this great moment. For the first lime I was seeing a being from
another world. His body was covered with a shiny metal foil­
pr sumably protection from cosmic rays."
   The 27-inch man, however, was no pushover. It took five men
to overpower him, according to Layne's data. Then, exhausted,
the invader passed out, was put in chains and given a stimulant.
(The captors, some think, had taken a stimulant too.)
   The critter put up a second fruitless fight after coming to, then
died suddenly-two hours from the moment of his landing./
   Where did he come from? Layne has an answer:
   He was a man from Etheria.
   Explains Layne, who has spent a lifetime probing the twilight
zone between science and fiction: "We are inhabitants of a
globe within the giant world of Etheria. San Diego happens to
be situated smack in the center of a great Etherian lake in the
heart of a great Etherian city. Why, waves are breaking over
our heads at this moment."
   If you wonder why we can't see or touch this world, Layne
has the answer. He reasons Etheria is entirely beyond the spec­
tra of sound, of sight, of touch.
   Peering at you with gentle eyes, Layne rounds out this theory:
"The Etherians keep archives on dying civilizations, such as
ours. They send out so-called flying saucers to reconnoiter and

  MORE ON                      ETHERIA
             Puffing a panatella in his bare Adams Avenue office,
          thin & scholarly Meade Layne found himself the center
          of controversy this week.
             Question: Was the first known photograph of a flying
          disc-man, which he released to POINT (Aug. 25), an
          honest lens job, or was it a retoucher's hoax?
             Layne, who is director of the Borderland Sciences
          Research Associates, faced the challenge by letter and
          even long-distance phone call. News of the 27-inch
          "aluminum man" (reprinted on the opposite page to
          meet the demand that sold out POINT's earlier issue 36
          hours after publication) spread across the nation when
          Frank Edwards, Mutual's Washington newscaster, de­
                        scribed him to uiillions of listeners.
                           The result: requests from all over the US
                        poured into POINT's offices, and Layne
                        was being pressured for more information
                        on the land of flying saucers-Etheria.
                          Layne, this week, came up with some­
                        thing better: more pictures.
                           Cautions Layne, whose office has re­
                        ceived in excess of 2000 reports of mys­
                        terious sky objects from the far-flung mem­
                        bership of his organization: "There seems
                        reason for accepting these pictures as
                        genuine. I am personally convinced that
                        disc-shaped crafi, with their operators, have
                        made a number of landings, and that these

                                                          FORTNIGHT, December 10, 1951
  soft climate of the inland town which
  nestles in the heart of San Diego'County.
  It's' a peaceful enough community, yet
  there's enough going on to keep people
  hustling.
   ' There's a scad of things for Escondido­
  ans to boast about and, with pardonable
  pride, they are prone to do it on occasions.
  It's just 15 miles to the beaches of the
. Pacific; a few miles in another direction
  is fine fishing; four miles the other way is
  Lake Wohlford; the desert resort of Borrego
  Springs is just off down the road a spell.
  For those interested, there are also the
  historic San Luis and Pala Missions. And,
  not to be forgotten, Del Mar racetrack is
  a hop over the hill. Being the focal point
  for such diversified goings-on is a source
  of satisfaction to the local folk.
     One of the biggest lures for a weekend
  motorist out of LA is Mt. Palomar, which
  Escondido seems to f-eel is just another
  feature set up to make the town more
  interesting. The local boosters have dubbed
  the town Gateway to the Stall.S as an ex-




    Not a telescope to peer through
             but a mirror.
 pression of their feelings about Palomar.
     The 200-inch telescope is the world's
 largest camera for studying the stars. It's
 four times as large as the next biggest but
 -so that no one will be disillusioned­
 it's not a gadget which you can peer
 through. It's for photo work only. Visitors
 view the telescope from a glass-enclosed
 cage--getting too close can raise havoc,
 as the heat from one's· body can throw the
 adjustments off!
     The telescope does enlarge the stars
 some. But its prime task is to collect light
 from the most distant star which-aimed
 at a photographic plate for hours'-some­
 times can give astronomers a permanent
 record of what's going on in the heavens.
  It's a $7 million camera.
     So Escondido sits happily back, pleased
 that it's surrounded by farms and resorts
 and seashores and mountains and science
  and history. It knows where it's been in
  the si;heme of things and knows where

   The evidence is overwhelming
that they are flying machines of
some sort.Too many competent ob­
servers have identified them as
such for any doubt to remain on
that point. Take, for example, the
experience of Captain Lawrence W.
Vinther, a pilot in the employ of
  Mid-Continent Airlines, who tan­
gled with one of the things not so
long ago.
   Captain Vinther was in charge of
a DC-3; his co-pilot "(_as. James F.
Bachner, a veteran flyer of World
War II with 6,000 hours of commer­
cial flying to his credit.They were
about to take off from Sioux City,
Iowa airport at 8:30 P.M. when the
flight-control tower requested that
they investigate a brilliant light in
the sky, traveling north-to-south
at an altitude of about 8,000 feet.
The light was to the west of the
airport.
    Note the . detail of this request,
which was quickly verified.. The
light was approached and found to
be where it was first located, allow­
ing for the fact that it was travel­
ing at a leisurely pace. But as the
DC-3 closed in it abruptly dived
over the nose of the approaching
plane, whirled about or reversed its
direction of flight almost instan­
taneously, and flew in formation
 with the DC-3 at a distance of
 about 200 feet, maintaining the
 same altitude and speed. It kept
 this up for about five seconds, after
 which-=as though satisfied with its

PICTURE OF" "SAUCERS" was submitted to LIFE by reader of April 7 ar­
ticle. But geophysicist has established it as a special type of cloud formation.




       SAUCER REACTIONS
They range from plausible theories to nonsense
            by ROBERT E. GINNA JR.
The April 7, 1952 issue of Lim, in which Bradford Darrach and I ex­
amined "the case for flying saucers," provoked a tremendaus barrage
of lelters. Some have been nonsensical, some philosophical, some have
contained provocative and plausible theories. Not only has the story
prompted an unprecedented response from the readers, but more and
more letters are still coming in.
   Many readers are apparently resigned to visitations from space al­
ready and expect a landing momentarily."We should start construc­
tion of a suitable landing field for them," declared one reader. Others
believe flying saucers to be far more than a study for scientists."God
is trying lo tell the world something," says one reader. Another adds
   rkly, "He has sent the final sign.... "
   Fr om the c ·             U.S.Air Force's saucer-investigating project
the article brought a note o appreciation for ne ping fueir i11Vesl1ga­
tions. "A considerable number of observers have written to us with
valuable information," he wrote, "because they were encouraged by
     LIFE article." And the further reports that have since om in will
continue to help the project. One in particular concerns the celebrated
"Lubbock Lights," which LIFE reported as having been seen racing
frequently over Lubbock, Texas. The profes or who saw them as­
sumed the altitude was 50,000 feel, noted their rate of change wa 30°
of arc per second, and accordingly estimated the lights' speed at 18,000
mph.Now Dr. R. S.Underwood, of the Department of Mathematics
at Texas Technological College, has written LIFE that he was able to
triangulate them on a September night last year and concluded that
their altitude was about 2,100 feet.This means that the lights' speed
was about 750 mph-a piece of information that may bring the Air
Force one more solid piece of evidence.
   Another contribution was in the form of a series of photographs
which Robert Retzinger took near Palm Springs, Calif. last March.
Dr. Ronald Ives, distingui hed geophysicist of Cornell Aeronautical
Laboratory, studied the pictur s and concluded that they showed the
generation of a Cumulus lenticularis, or lens-shaped loud. This type
of cloud, common in the area, is formed, hen compressed and heated
air pushes up moist air so that it condenses into lens-shaped clouds.
The clouds are often sheared into sections by higher winds, as can be
seen in the picture at the top of the page. It is easy to see how a cloud
like this, reflecting the lights below, might be taken for a flying saucer.
   There was, of course, a minority of readers who dissented from the
conclusions in the article. Some still argued that the saucers were super­
secret U.S.weapons; LIFE's article had dismissed this argument on the
ground that the government would hardly allow one branch of the
service to spend vast sums of money on a saucer investigation which
would have the primary effect of fooling another government branch
even more completely than the enemy. Others maintained that the
evidence was not precise enough, although the article had pointed out

South Africa, in July 1943. His
description agrees in nearly ev­
ery respect with the bizarre green
fireballs seen in the American
Southwest five years later. As­

green meteor , it gives pause

   3. The Air Force hopes to put
radar in the flying saucer hunt on
a big scale. Radar sightings have
been recorded at key places like
 Oak Ridge, Tenn., and Goose Bay,
 Labrador. ATIC can never be cer­

stem from a sighted object, weath­
er conditions or equipment mal­
 functions. By combining existing
 radar, telescopes and cameras, pho­
 tographs can be taken of any solid
 objects spotted in the daytime and
 of glowing objects at night.

HOW DO SAUCERS FLY_?
                            I ( '




    Most flying saucen have been reported seen in almost the same area, that of western United States.

"                                                                                          PIC, November, 1952
                      By John W. Campbell, Jr.
                                     NUCLEAR PHYSICIST
                                     AND SCIENCE EDITOR




                                 T   HE TROUBLE with flying saucers is that what they
                                     do doesn't seem to make sense, it's been difficult to get
                                 pictures of them or communicate with them, and yet
                                 anybody-any people-who can build• such marvelous
                                 machines must be sensible-supremely sensible indeed.
                                 There mu.st be some completely reasonable explanation
                                 for the purpose behind their curious behavior.
                                    Those machines represent a science so far ahead of
                                 ours that it's on a different level. The workings of elec­
                                 tronics and radar and radio would have thrown Isaac
                                 Newton, Michael Faraday, and the great scientists of the
                                 1850's-1880's for a compfete and total loss. The electron
                                 wasn't discovered until after 1890; whole realms of
                                 science were unguessed at that time.
                                    Of course, we, today, ere much smarter. We know all
                                 those things ... but no man can ever guess how much he
                                 doesn't know. Dalton, the English chemist who developed
                                 the atomic theory of chemical reaction in its �odem
                                 form, never dreamed that the "atoms" he talked of were
                                 more complex structures than the chemicals he knew!
                                   We don't know, and can't possibly guess, how much
                                 we do NOT know-until somebody goes blithely ·skim­
                                 ming along overhead in a flying saucer.
                                   The saucer's don't have wings; they don't have rockets,
                                jets, propellors, or any other known gadget. Quite liter­
                                 ally, they have "no visible means of support." No law of
                                 nature known to present science can explain them. And
                                 people who know more science than we do are, quite·
                                 evidently, not appreciably less intelligent than we are
                                ourselves. (Nor are they, necessarily, any more1 intelli­
                                gent. Without increasing our intelligence, another 100
                                 years of science will yield a lot more knowledge.)
                                   Flying saucers, by their very existence, indic�te some­
                                body with brains that really work is flitting around up
                                in the sky. But tpeir actions are so strange-so seemingly
                                illogical! Why, if they can, don't they establish communi­
                                catjon with us? And surely, minds that can figure out
                                such marvelous machines can figure out how to establish
                                communication.
                                   No one has ever taken a satisfactory picture of the
                                saucer. There have been some exceedingly poor, badly:
                                focused, blurred and distorted snapshots-but they're
                                useless. Why-in view of the literally thousands of �ight­
                                ings-haven't there been pict.,ures? Are the saucers real,
                                after all?
                                   They are real. The reason for lack of pictures is easy
                                to understand; they fly either low and fast, or high and
                                slow. A machine flying 600 to 1000 miles an hour at an
                                elevation of 1,000 feet or so is in sight for a few seconds.
                                At 10,000 feet, even if the ship is loafing along at 100
                                miles an hour, you can't take a photograph that's any
                                good, unless you use an enormous camera with a 48-inch­
                                loRg telescopic lens. And that      (Continued on page 73)

W         hat it is, where it comes from, how it files no
          one knows. The only thing that is known is
  that it exists; and the only thing that every-
  one seems to agree on is that it looks somewhat
  like a plate. Beyond this, speculation runa the
  gamut of foreign weapons, ships from another planet,
  weather disturbances, remote-controlled missiles and
· odd saucers looking for cups. The disc-shaped objects
  are claimed to have been seen by persons in all parts
  of the United States, by flyers in Japan, citizens in
  Germany, Labrador, and most recently in Brazil.
     It was at 4:30 P.M. on the seventh of May, 1952,
  that O Cruziero's Joao :Martins and Ed Keffel, on
  assignment some 18 kilometers west of Sugar Loa!,
  saw "an object moving in the air, on the aide of the
  eun . . . at a distance it looked like an airplane,
  but it moved to one side at tremendous epeed."
  According to the photographers, "The circular, bluish­
  grey object decreased its speed, loet altitude like a
   falling leaf and, like an arrow, took off again
   towarde high seas."
     On these pages are Keffel's pictur«)&-proof that
  the men were not suffering from hallucinations.

               A NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SocmTv expedition in the Mediterra­
               nean Sea off the southern coast of France has discovered and is
               now raising the oldest known cargo ship in the world, a Greco­
               Roman vessel sunk in the third century before Christ, Dr. Gilbert
               Grosvenor, president of the Society has announced. Almost 1,000
               large amphoras-pottery vessels used to carry the liquid cargoes
               of the ancients-have been recovered. Some, still corked, con­
               tained wine more than 2,100 years old.

     My reasons fo,: writing this article:
     First to clarify and prove once and for all that "Fl,ying
  Sauce-rs'' are real and· of tangible .S1,bstance. Secondly, and
  above all, to help free persons seeing unidentified aerial ob­
  jects from being ridiculed by press and radio. Instead, after
  reading this article, they should be encouraged to make such
  reports.
    l think it is high time for �e Air Force to acknowledge that
� saucers exist, and by maki11g this acknowledgement they will
  receive the full cooperation of every citizen in reporting
  sightings. Only with the cooperation of the entire nation can
  we find out if these things are hostile or friendly.-Ralph
  Mayher.

                By    RALPH         MAYHER

 �E a1-ticle you are about to read has been kept from
       ��u, the American public, for twenty-two months.
       Now at long last, in my-own words and photographs,
 I will explain what happened on the night of July 29,
 1952.
    I am able to give you this true story now because I
 have removed the uniform as a United States Marine and
 I 'can speak freely as an American civilian.
    Since the end of the second world war there have been
 numerous reports of disks and balls of fire floating through
 the sky. I (like most everyone else) gave these reports
 very little thought or attention. Reports increased and
 somewhere along the line the objects acquired the name
 of ":[,'lying Saucers." Therefore throughout this article I        Ralph Mayher, Richard Boswell and Mrs. Mayher re-enact
                   (Cqntinued on next page)                         the scene when saucer was sighted and p,hotographed.

                                                       will refer to these strange objects as "Flying Saucers."
                                                        ( Officially there is no such thing.)
                                                           Throughout the years of 1948 and 194� I read much
                                                       about Flying Saucers. Our Atomic tests increased in
                                                       number and more saucer stories appeared. In early 1950
                                                       I no longer thought there was any need for Flying Saucer
                                                       jokes. The matter had become important to us, our gov­
                                                       ernment, and the world.
                                                          Then came the Korean War. On February 8, 1952, I
                                                       was inducted into the United States Marine Corps and I
                                                       was very proud to serve with the finest. With my photo­
                                                       graphic background I was sent directly from boot camp
                                                       at Parris Island, South Carolina, to a new Air Station at
                                                       Opa-Locka, Florida. This base is on the outskirts of
                                                       Miami.
                                                           During the months of May and June of 1952 saucer
                                                       reports in the state of Flol'ida were incredibly high. A
                                                       good example of this occurred at a Key West outdoor
                                                       theater. Over one hundred sailors saw· a saucer hover
                                                       and then disappear into space. The interest became so
                                                       intense that Miami television station WTVJ posted a one
                                                       hundred dollar reward to any cameraman furnishing the
                                                       station with a picture of a saucer in the Miami area.
                                                           On July 28, 1952, an amazing sigh ting was reported in
                                                       the Miami Daily News and by WTVJ. The late Mr. Gold­
                                                       stein of Tatem Waterway, Miami Beach, had seen a saucer
                                                       at such a low altitude it appeared to be as large as a full
                                                       moon. I interviewed Mr. Goldstein. He was obviously
                                                       sincere.

   "Their impression, however, was that the object re­

   I give my thanks to Jim Ward, formerly with WIOD
and now with WITV, for the tape recording he made
which carried all facts and was beamed over the state
of Florida.
   Jokingly I asked Mr. Ward, "I wonder what they will
use for cloud reflection stories when there were no clouds
on the beach?"
   That evening I appeared on the Ralph Renick news
show. The TV cameras flashed one frame of my movie
film. The next day people began calling the newspaper
and radio station demanding an explanation.
   Over 22 months have passed and still no official com­
ment on the movies.
   The three photos shown here were taken from three
consecutive frames of the 16 mm film. These pictures are
 released for publication to PIC magazine for the first time
and have copyright applied for. (Note change in shape.)
Time was one/forty-fifth of a second between each view.
   The accompanying formula (shown in photostat letters)
was worked out by Dr. Rainwater, assistant professor of
physics, University of Miami.
   The 2000-foot altitude computed is quite accurate be­
cause the two officers, Commander Gardner and Lt. Com­
 mander Mills, agree that whatever they saw was parallel
 to their own altitude of approximately 2000 feet. (I am
assuming this was the same object I photographed.) The
 weather report from the U.S. weather bureau at Miami
had reported widely scattered clouds at approximately
 3000 feet. Many observers in Hialeah said they saw the
object pass through one of those low-hanging clouds.
 I assume the disk stayed at this same altitude as it crossed
 from Miami Beach to Hialeah.
    I finally wrote a letter to the Air Force which has been
 studying my film for over a year. Here is the unanswered
 copy of that letter:
                                                Oct. 16, 1953
 Operation Blue Book
 Air Technical Intelligence Center
 Wright-Patterson Field,
 Dayton, Ohio
 Dear Sir:
    After reading the book "Flying Saucers from Outer

                                                                                            AT 2:24, A.M. ON September 3, 1965,
                                                                                            Norman Muscarello walked into the
                                                                                            Exeter, . H., police station, appar­
                                                                                            ently near shock. Patrolman Reginald
                                                                                            Toland, who was on duty at the desk,
                                                                                            helped him light a cigarette before
                                                                                            Muscarello was calm enough to talk.
                                                                                                He had been hitchhiking north on
                                                                                            Route 150 from Amesbury, Mass., to
  Was it delusion? Or did more than 60 people living near                                   hi; home in Exeter, a distance of 12
                                                                                            miles. T he traffic was sparse, he said,

                                                                                            pulsating red lights outlining an ap­
                                                                                            parent rim. It wobbled, yawed and
                                                                                            floated toward him, but made no
                                                                                            noise whatever. He was afraid it was
                                                                                            going to hit him and protected him­
                                                                                            self by diving into the shallow shoul­
                                                                                            der of the road.
                                                                                                T he object backed off slowly and
                                                                                            hovered directly over the roof of one
                                                                                            of the two nearby houses. Finally, it
                                                                                            backed off far enough for Muscarello
                                                                                            Lo make a run for one of the houses.
                                                                                            He pounded on the door, screaming.
                                                                                              1o one answ 0red. At that moment, a

                                                                                            middle-aged couple picked him up,
                                                                                            took him into Exeter and dropped

                                                                                            you don't believe me. I don't blame

said to execute defy the force of earthly

survive comparable maneuvers. Is there
some way to cancel the pull of gravity?
Earthmen have been hunting one for a
long time, with no success.
   Because of these fundamental theo­
retical barriers to undetected invasion
of the earili by space vehicles, conserva­
tive physical scientists shy from involve­
ment in the UFO hunt. That is why the
Science and Ash·onautics Committee of
the Congress has never been willing to
hold publi hearings on the question. It
is why the National Aeronautics and
Spac Administration has held aloof. It
is why the National Academy of Sci­
ences has declined suggestions to ap­
point an investigative panel.
   It could be argued that there is little
or no scientific justification for continued
dignification of UFOs. But the question
has extended itself well beyond the
range of pure science. The credibility of
the Air Force is deeply involved, and the
only way to clear the air is to employ
whatever science may be employed le­
gitimately. The recommendations of the
